extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners solving linear differential equations and classical geometry problems (advanced undergraduate / mathematical problem-solvers)
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and operational identities for integrating linear differential equations using operator manipulations (conjugation by exponentials, factorization of operator polynomials, series/terminating expansions), together with worked classical-geometry solution methods illustrating sine-rule manipulations, pole-polar constructions, coordinate reductions and symmetry arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator conjugation identity (exponential shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: e^{-∫X dx} D e^{∫X dx} y = (D + X) y (and analogous identities for powers and negative powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjugation by e^{∫X dx} to transform the differential operator D into D+X when it acts on y. This generalises to higher and negative powers: replacing y by e^{∫X dx}y moves the X-term to the operator acting on the transformed function. Employ this to divide an equation by an operator factor and to find its effect on the second member. Example: e^{-∫X dx} (D^n) e^{∫X dx} = (D+X)^n acting on y. Anti-pattern: forgetting that the exponentials act on subsequent factors and functions; do not drop the conjugation step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of non-commuting operator factors matters
rubrics_metrics.description: When operator factors are of the form (D + β)(D + α) with coefficient-functions, changing the order of these factors generally changes the equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reorder operator factors unless they commute. Only when the product corresponds to the same polynomial f(D) (i.e., treating f(D) as a polynomial in D whose factorization into linear factors corresponds to roots) can one reorder factors without changing the overall operator polynomial; otherwise the sequence of operations changes the differential equation. Practical consequence: when dividing/operating sequentially, respect the original factor order unless you have justified commutativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorization into linear operator factors to obtain first-order equations (Boole's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f(D) factors as ∏(D + X - r_i) (r_i roots of f(x)=0), then by dividing by all but one factor (without operating on the RHS) we obtain first-order equations (D + X - r_i) y = 0, each giving a particular integral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use factorization to reduce higher-order linear equations to simpler first-order factors whose integrals are easier to find. This is especially useful when f(D) is a polynomial in D with identifiable roots. Note: when the product of factors equals the same polynomial, the equation remains the same for any order of those factors (commutative product viewed as polynomial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of infinite-product / series expansions for negative operator powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative powers of operator expressions can be handled by expanding using repeated conjugation and infinite continued multiplications; summing constants multiplied by these continued results yields expressions for /(D + X) y involving expansions continued to infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dividing by an operator expressed with negative powers, expand by applying the conjugation identity repeatedly, multiply results by constants, and sum to obtain the desired expression. Practical note: such expansions may converge or be formal; check conditions (e.g., when the operator function is a polynomial the expansion may terminate).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator translation theorem: e^{x a} f(D) e^{-x a} = f(D + a)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjugating an operator-function f(D) by exponentials in x translates the argument of f by the exponential's coefficient: e^{ax} f(D) e^{-ax}y = f(D + a) y (and generalisations with operator-valued increments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exponential conjugation to 'shift' D to D+a, so that an operator depending on D becomes one depending on D+a; useful when f(D+a) is simpler to integrate. The text gives generalisations where the shift itself can be operator-valued (e.g., 0'(D)D'). Choose the form that makes one member of the equation easiest to integrate and use the other member to recover y. Example formulas labelled (D), (E), (F) illustrate this principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose to integrate the easier member after operator manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply operator identities (C),(D),(E),(F) to rewrite the equation so that one member becomes easy to integrate; integrate that member and then use the relation to find the unknown function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical strategy: apply suitable conjugation/translation so the left-hand operator acting on y becomes a simple differential (or polynomial in D) whose integral is known; then invert the conjugation to obtain y. This is essentially a tactical guideline: pick the form of operator manipulation based on which side yields a tractable integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Termination of expansions when operator-functions are polynomials (integer functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ(D) is an integer (polynomial) function of D, expansions of operator expressions terminate and are easily integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When φ(D) is a polynomial in D, the series arising from expanding composite operator expressions will be finite (terminate after finitely many terms). Prefer algebraic manipulation in these cases because integration reduces to a finite combination of derivatives/integrals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separability when different differential operators act on different variables (Di, Dj)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Di operates on x only and Dj on y only, then φ(Di + Dj) expands into a finite series φ(Di) + φ'(Di)Dj + ... which often terminates, reducing the PDE/integral to iterated one-variable problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit operator separation when variables are decoupled by assigning distinct differential operators to each variable. Expand φ(Di + Dj) as a series in Dj with coefficients involving Di; if the series terminates, integrate by treating the resulting equation as an ODE in one variable with parameter dependence on the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling composite operator equations by substitution of operator modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ1(D)/ψ(D) φ2(D)/ψ(D) y = 0 (composition of operator-quotients), obtain integrals and expansions by replacing y with ψ(D)/... y and permuting symbols accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When operators compose via quotients or substitutions, derive integrals of the composite equation by mapping to previously solved forms: change D and related operators into the new operator symbols and change y into the transformed dependent function. Use this to reuse known solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator action on products: interpret D+D' appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing D + D' it may denote D operating on both X and y (or on all that follows), enabling re-interpretation of composite actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful about the intended scope of differential operators in expressions like D + D'. Clarify whether D acts on the product (both factors) or whether separate operators act on separate factors. Correct interpretation can simplify manipulation (e.g., allow replacement of D + D' by a single D in a given context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated integration by parts to generate series expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated application of integration by parts yields series representations of integrals (illustrated for ∫ e^{x} dx and related integrals), useful for asymptotic expansions or closed-form series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply integration by parts repeatedly to express ∫ e^{x} f(x) dx as an alternating series of derivatives/integrals; watch boundary terms and convergence (limits such as x→0 may make terms vanish). Useful for generating power-series expansions of integrals and for obtaining known expansions by choosing the sequence of parts appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trigonometric/sine-rule products and telescoping to prove collinearity for copolar triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: To show that intersection points of constructed lines lie on a straight line (copolar triangles), form sine-ratio relations for each constructed segment, multiply the ratios and use properties of copolar triangles (e.g., CA_i·BC_i·AB_i = CB_i·BA_i·AC_i) to obtain equality implying collinearity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: write sine-law ratios for corresponding segments formed by parallels/constructed lines, take the product of resulting relations, use known equalities from copolar-triangle properties to cancel terms and obtain a proportion of the form PB2·QA2·RC2 = PA2·QC2·RB2; interpret this as the projective/collinearity condition in the auxiliary triangle. This is a template for many classical geometry proofs involving cyclicity, similarity and product-of-ratios arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetry and coefficient-vanishing argument for surfaces through parallelepiped vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: To show all quadric surfaces through the eight vertices of a parallelepiped have the same centre (intersection of diagonals) and conjugate diameters parallel to edges, impose the conditions at the eight corner points to deduce vanishing of certain cross terms and translate the origin to the centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: write general quadratic surface ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + d yz + e zx + f xy + g x + h y + k z + 1 = 0, evaluate at the eight corner coordinates, take linear combinations (sums/differences) of those evaluations to deduce that linear and mixed coefficients vanish, so the equation reduces to a centered diagonal quadratic. Then translate origin to intersection of body diagonals to see conjugate diameters align with edges. This is a standard symmetry-reduction technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive method for triangle from given sum of two sides, inradius, and base-angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the sum of the two sides, the inradius and one base angle, construct the triangle by tangent/pole constructions: draw the given circle tangent at a point, construct tangents and auxiliary right/angle lines, use parallels and circle arcs to locate vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipe: draw circle touching base at given point, through centre construct angle equal to supplement of given base angle, draw tangent at appropriate point and measure off the given sum of sides along it; construct auxiliary perpendiculars/bisectors and a circle through chosen auxiliary points so its intersection with base determines vertex B; finally draw tangent from B to obtain the triangle. The proof uses tangent properties and equal tangents from centre to show the summed sides equal the chosen segment. This is a template for geometric construction problems involving tangency and length constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional-ratio reasoning for commerce/fractional-profit problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When portions of a commodity are sold at different percentage profits and an overall percentage profit is known, equate weighted averages (or view differences from mean) to obtain ratios of quantities sold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: compare each portion's profit deviation from overall mean profit; the quantities sold are in inverse proportion to those deviations. Example: if first profit is 25% (35% below mean) and second is 175% (115% above mean) with overall 60%, then sold quantities are in ratio 115:35, from which absolute sizes follow when additional fixed-volume information is supplied. This ‘allegation’/weighted average trick is a standard short method in profit-mixture problems.
